kakekotoba.interaction: 九重 literally means 'ninefold' and is a fixed term for the Imperial Palace/capital (Kyoto), while also numerically echoing and contrasting with 八重 (eightfold) in the kami-no-ku — the poem plays on the numerical progression from eight-layered blossoms to the nine-layered palace, so the word simultaneously denotes the physical place (the palace) and completes the numerical wordplay begun by yae-zakura. This is not a strict homophonic pivot but a paronomastic number-play that functions similarly, linking the two halves through arithmetic/verbal echo rather than two unrelated lexical meanings, so it is included here as a borderline case of double-signification central to the poem's wit.

bipartite.kami_theme: The ancient capital of Nara and its famous eightfold cherry blossoms — an image of a bygone era's beauty
bipartite.shimo_theme: Today, in the ninefold palace of the present capital (Kyoto), those very blossoms bloom in fragrant splendor
bipartite.pivot_note: The poem pivots from a nostalgic evocation of the old Nara capital's celebrated yae-zakura to the present moment, in which those same (or descended) blossoms have been brought to bloom within the imperial court at the new capital — collapsing past and present, and old and new capitals, into a single image of continuity and flourishing. The numerical wordplay (八重→九重) reinforces the sense of the past blossoming anew, more richly, in the present.

kigo.note: Yae-zakura, the double-flowered cherry blossom, is one of the most celebrated spring flowering images in classical waka, associated with abundance and courtly splendor; here it also carries historical resonance tying Nara's ancient glory to the present flourishing of the Heian court.
